fetched_contents.text: Did mandatory IFRS adoption affect the cost of capital in Latin American countries? Introduction The movement towards mandating the adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) is considered the most widespread global financial reform in accounting history (Daske, Hail, Leuz, & Verdi, 2008). The premise of these standards is to improve the transparency and reliability of financial statements across the globe and facilitate cross border investments. As a result of this global dimension, determining the economic consequences of the accounting standards as part of financial regulatory reforms is both more challenging and important as more countries with diverse levels of development adopt IFRS (Zeff, 2012). A considerable body of literature investigates the economic effects of IFRS adoption in developed nations (Barth, Landsman, & Lang, 2008; Daske et al., 2008; Houqe, Monem, & Zijl, 2016).1 They report the consequences of the adoption of IFRS on several different users, including accountants, investors, analysts, governments and international regulators. However, few studies have investigated these effects in the Latin American context (Pelucio-Grecco, Geron, Grecco, & Lima, 2014; Rodríguez García, del, Cortez Alejandro, Méndez Sáenz, & Garza Sánchez, 2017). Examining these effects have significant potential economic and social implications for emerging countries, which can impact both national and international users of accounting information. Therefore, regulators are interested in whether adopting IFRS may have contributed toward reducing the cost of capital and consequentially signalling an increase in market efficiency and market liquidity (Han, Tang, & Yang, 2016). Investors are interested in whether information asymmetry problems were reduced after IFRS adoption. This would signal lower effort in acquiring and verifying information, allowing for more efficient investment decisions (Ball, 2006; Diamond & Verrecchia, 1991) and a potential increase in cross-border investments (DeFond, Hu, Hung, & Li, 2011). Overall, these potential enhancements to the economic conditions of these countries are argued to ‘improve people’s lives’ (Turley, 2007). However, there are increasing calls to provide empirical evidence on the impact of these standards on emerging countries. The limited literature about Latin America focuses on the impact of IFRS on accounting quality, but the economic consequences of such adoption are yet to be fully explored. To fill this gap in the literature, we investigate the impact of IFRS adoption on the cost of equity and the cost of debt in Latin American countries. There are several reasons of exploring the economic consequences of IFRS in Latin America. First, Latin American countries have two economic trading blocs, the Mercado Comum do Sul (MERCOSUL)2 and the Pacific Alliance,3 which both aim to promote free trade among their participants. Through these blocs, commodities are exchanged with developed countries, and investment opportunities are created particularly by attracting foreign direct investment, from countries such as the United States (US) and China (Trevino, Thomas, & Cullen, 2008; Tuman & Emmert, 2004).4 Thus, the mandatory adoption of IFRS leads to changes in accounting standards, which in turn can affect the way foreign investors make their investment decisions in the worldwide economy. Indeed, this is a significant step taken by the governments of these countries to develop their capital markets through the adoption of ‘high-quality’ accounting standards to benefit investors, analysts, lenders, and other users of accounting.5 Second, studying Latin American markets also allows us to investigate the determinants and effects of reporting quality and its economic consequences in different national institutional settings, as these typically have variations in the enforcement of accounting standards, different investor protection mechanisms, and lesser-developed capital markets (Ball, 2016). Previous literature focusing mainly on developed countries demonstrate that reporting quality and its economic effects are not determined by the adoption of high-quality accounting standards per se, but vary according to the level of legal enforcement, investors’ protection and managers’ incentives (Ball, Robin, & Wu, 2003; Barth et al., 2008; Christensen, Hail, & Leuz, 2013). The enforcement and investor protection mechanisms in Latin American countries are weak (Brown, Preiato, & Tarca, 2014; La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer, & Vishny, 1998), and have not changed significantly since the mandatory IFRS adoption (Moura & Gupta, 2019). This institutional environment is optimal for identifying more clearly the impact of the IFRS adoption on the cost of capital. Thus, investigating the Latin American case can extend the international literature, and answer the call of the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) for evidence on the economic consequences and impact of adopting IFRS in emerging markets. We examine firms from five Latin American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, México, and Peru).6 The other countries could not be included as they either adopted IFRS after 2014 or their empirical data was not available. We calculate the cost of debt following Moscariello, Skerratt, and Pizzo (2014), and the cost of equity based on the average of four methods proposed in previous literature (Claus & Thomas, 2001; Easton, 2004; Gebhardt, Lee, & Swaminathan, 2001; Gode & Mohanram, 2003). The measures of cost of equity and debt are compared four years prior to and after the official date of mandatory IFRS adoption. This paper documents that IFRS contributed significantly to reducing the cost of equity and the cost of debt in Latin American markets. We also find some weak evidence that firm-level reporting incentives affect to a certain degree the cost of equity. This paper provides the first insights into the impact of IFRS on the cost of capital…

fetched_contents.text: Meta‐analysis of the Impact of Adoption of IFRS on Financial Reporting Comparability, Market Liquidity, and Cost of Capital Author Listed: * Solomon Opare * Muhammad Nurul Houqe * Tony van Zijl Abstract A large number of empirical studies have addressed the effects of adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), but the results have been mixed. We use a meta‐analysis of 56 empirical studies with 1,265 effect sizes to determine the impact of adoption of IFRS on financial reporting comparability, market liquidity, cost of equity, and cost of debt. This approach provides an objective view of the empirical results, in contrast to narrative reviews which offer subjective conclusions. We find that IFRS adoption has increased financial reporting comparability and market liquidity, and reduced the cost of equity. For cost of debt, a decrease is observed only for voluntary adoption. Our meta‐regression analysis explains the variation in the observed effect of adoption of IFRS across mandatory and voluntary adoption of IFRS, and choice of measures, control variables, estimation methods, and the strength of the empirical results. We emphasize the importance of these study characteristics and call for further studies focusing on the cost of debt and also studies using recent data to reflect the changes in IFRS. This study should be of interest to regulators and policymakers as they are expected to assess the impacts of adoption of IFRS. Empirical evidence on liquidity improvements after IFRS adoption is mixed but suggestive of real effects in some samples and settings. The strongest direct evidence comes from Bonsall et al. (2024), which explicitly investigates whether less liquid firms benefited more from mandatory IFRS adoption and finds liquidity benefits for EU bundled firms, especially those with the lowest liquidity, as well as for EU firms in high and low regulatory quality countries, with stronger benefits for the lowest liquidity firms in some cases [N1-F1]. This study is important because it attempts to isolate IFRS effects from other concurrent regulatory changes, suggesting that the observed liquidity improvements are more likely attributable to IFRS adoption itself [N1-F1].

A second line of evidence comes from the meta-analysis, which reports that IFRS adoption has increased market liquidity overall and that the effect is heterogeneous across studies and specifications [N5-F3]. This supports the idea that liquidity gains are not universal but are present in the aggregate empirical literature. The review also notes that the literature includes country-month liquidity analysis, which strengthens the ability to assess cross-country and cross-time liquidity effects [N4-R5].

The liquidity measures used in the evidence base are not fully consistent across studies. Bonsall et al. uses liquidity benefits framed in terms of transaction costs and method-of-moments quantile regression, and the abstract emphasizes that the effects are observed in relation to firms that did not adopt IFRS by the end of 2005 [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis does not specify exact liquidity metrics in the excerpted material, so its evidence is more general than the Bonsall paper [N5-F3]. Other sources in the search set emphasize market liquidity and comparability as the outcome variables, but the specific liquidity measures used in individual studies are not clearly identified in the provided excerpts [N4-R1, N4-R4, N4-R5].

On country and sample strength, the evidence points to EU settings and Latin America as particularly informative. Bonsall et al. finds the strongest liquidity benefits in EU bundled firms and EU firms from low regulatory quality countries, with the lowest liquidity firms showing the largest gains [N1-F1]. The Latin American study in the search set is described as examining firms from Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, and Peru and using firm-year panel regression [N2-F2]. While the excerpt does not give detailed results, it positions Latin America as a useful context for testing IFRS effects because of weak enforcement and different institutional settings [N2-F2]. The review of IFRS adoption literature also stresses that heterogeneity is important and that effects vary by country and setting [N4-R5].

The effect is concentrated in less liquid firms in the evidence base. Bonsall et al. is explicit that the lowest liquidity firms benefited the most, and that liquidity benefits were especially pronounced for those firms [N1-F1]. This is a central finding in the provided material and suggests that IFRS adoption may be more valuable for firms where information asymmetry is higher and liquidity is lower [N1-F1]. The literature review also notes firm-level heterogeneity in liquidity effects, consistent with the idea that not all firms experience the same magnitude of improvement [N4-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports statistically significant liquidity improvements in some samples, but the strength of the effect varies by country, regulatory quality, and firm liquidity. The measures are not fully standardized across studies, and the strongest effects appear to be concentrated in less liquid firms, particularly in EU and low-regulatory-quality settings [N1-F1][N4-R5].

Empirical evidence on cost-of-capital reductions after IFRS adoption is also mixed but overall supportive of reductions in both equity and debt, with some caveats. The meta-analysis reports that IFRS adoption has reduced the cost of equity and that a decrease is observed only for voluntary adoption for cost of debt [N5-F3]. This suggests that cost-of-capital effects are not uniform across adoption types and that the literature is more robust for equity capital than for debt capital in the excerpted evidence.

The Latin American study is a direct example of a cost-of-capital reduction. It finds that IFRS contributed significantly to reducing the cost of equity and the cost of debt in Latin American markets, with some weak evidence that firm-level reporting incentives also affect the cost of equity [N2-F2]. This is important because it provides a country-specific case where the cost-of-capital effect is positive and statistically significant, even though the debt effect is only weakly supported in the excerpted findings [N2-F2].

The cost-of-capital measures in the evidence base are constructed differently across studies. The Latin American study calculates the cost of debt following Moscariello, Skerratt, and Pizzo (2014), and the cost of equity based on the average of four methods proposed in previous literature: Claus and Thomas (2001), Easton (2004), Gebhardt et al. (2001), and Gode and Mohanram (2003) [N2-F2]. The meta-analysis does not give the exact debt measure in the excerpt, but it does emphasize that the effect is heterogeneous across mandatory and voluntary adoption and across measures and control variables [N5-F3]. This heterogeneity implies that the interpretation of cost-of-capital reductions depends on the specification and sample.

The evidence suggests that effects are somewhat robust across samples and specifications, but not universally so. The meta-analysis explicitly states that it uses 56 studies and 1,265 effect sizes to determine the impact of IFRS adoption and that meta-regression explains variation across mandatory and voluntary adoption, measures, control variables, estimation methods, and the strength of the empirical results [N5-F3]. This implies that the overall conclusion is robust in a broad sense, but individual studies may differ in magnitude and significance.

The debt and equity effects differ in the evidence base. The meta-analysis finds a clear cost-of-equity reduction but only a cost-of-debt reduction for voluntary adoption [N5-F3]. The Latin American study finds significant reductions in both cost of equity and cost of debt, but the excerpt emphasizes “weak evidence” for the cost of equity effect in relation to firm-level reporting incentives, suggesting that the debt effect is stronger or more consistent in the Latin American sample [N2-F2]. This divergence across studies indicates that the cost-of-capital effect is not uniform and may depend on the setting and the measure used.

Overall, the evidence supports cost-of-capital reductions, especially for equity capital, but the magnitude and robustness vary across studies. The cost-of-capital measure is constructed differently across studies, and the strongest evidence is more consistent for equity than for debt in the provided excerpted material [N5-F3][N2-F2].

The causal mechanisms linking IFRS adoption to liquidity and cost of capital are best understood as improvements in information quality, transparency, and comparability, which reduce information asymmetry and improve investor and analyst behavior. The literature review explicitly states that IFRS adoption enhances comparability and credibility of financial statements, reduces uncertainty, and reduces information asymmetry [N3-R3]. Another source argues that IFRS adoption improves information quality and comparability of financial statements and thus increases investors' interest in investing [N3-R5]. A separate study on IFRS, information asymmetry, and stock liquidity concludes that high trading volume is associated with lower levels of information asymmetry and increased stock liquidity, implying that transparency and liquidity are closely linked [N1-R4].

Investor and analyst behavior change after IFRS adoption because better financial reporting makes it easier for market participants to evaluate firms. The meta-analysis notes that IFRS adoption improves financial reporting comparability and market liquidity and reduces the cost of equity, while the literature review emphasizes that IFRS adoption contributes to a lower cost of capital by improving the information environment [N5-F3][N3-R3]. The Latin American study also frames IFRS adoption as contributing to lower effort in acquiring and verifying information, allowing for more efficient investment decisions and potentially increasing cross-border investments [N2-F2]. These behavioral changes are consistent with the idea that investors and analysts place more trust in standardized financial information after IFRS adoption.

The link between information asymmetry and market liquidity is direct and important. The search result on IFRS adoption, information asymmetry, and stock liquidity states that high trading volume is associated with lower levels of information asymmetry and increased stock liquidity [N1-R4]. This implies that information asymmetry is a key determinant of liquidity and that reducing information asymmetry should improve liquidity. The literature review further ties reduced information asymmetry to lower cost of capital, reinforcing the causal chain from IFRS adoption to better information quality to lower cost of capital [N3-R3].

Omitted variables and reverse causality problems are important caveats. The Bonsall et al. study is explicitly cautious about attributing liquidity benefits to IFRS adoption, noting that other concurrent regulatory changes and unobserved factors could explain the results [N1-F1]. The Latin American study is also described in a way that emphasizes the need to distinguish the effect of IFRS adoption from other institutional factors, especially in emerging markets where enforcement and investor protection mechanisms are weak [N2-F2]. The meta-analysis further notes that heterogeneity in the observed effect is explained by mandatory and voluntary adoption, choice of measures, control variables, estimation methods, and the strength of the empirical results [N5-F3]. These points suggest that the observed effects may not be entirely causal if omitted variables, reverse causality, or other confounding factors are not fully controlled for.

In short, the causal mechanisms are centered on improved information quality, transparency, and comparability, which reduce information asymmetry and improve investor and analyst behavior, thereby increasing market liquidity and reducing cost of capital. However, the evidence base also cautions against overinterpreting the results because omitted variables, reverse causality, and heterogeneous identification strategies can affect the observed effects [N3-R3][N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3].

The conditions under which IFRS adoption is more or less likely to improve liquidity and reduce cost of capital are shaped by country, institutional, market, and implementation factors. The strongest evidence in the provided material points to regulatory quality, enforcement, and institutional settings as important amplifiers. Bonsall et al. finds liquidity benefits for EU firms from low regulatory quality countries, with greater benefits for the lowest liquidity firms, and also for non-EU firms from low regulatory quality countries [N1-F1]. This suggests that in countries with weaker regulatory environments, the gains from IFRS adoption may be more pronounced because the baseline information asymmetry is higher and the need for standardized reporting is stronger [N1-F1].

Adoption timing and implementation quality matter because the Latin American study explicitly examines firms from countries that adopted IFRS after 2014 and notes that data availability limited inclusion of other countries [N2-F2]. ### 6) Integrated conclusion

Empirical studies explain the conditions under which mandatory IFRS adoption improves liquidity and reduces the cost of capital as follows:

- **Positive effects are likely when IFRS adoption improves information quality, transparency, and comparability**, reducing information asymmetry and improving investor and analyst behavior [N3-R3][N3-R5][N1-R4].
- **Liquidity improvements are most pronounced in less liquid firms**, especially in EU bundled firms and EU firms from low regulatory quality countries, with the lowest liquidity firms benefiting the most [N1-F1].
- **Cost-of-capital reductions are supported for equity capital and sometimes for debt capital, but the effects are heterogeneous and depend on the measure and sample** [N5-F3][N2-F2].
- **The effects are stronger in countries with weak regulatory quality, low enforcement, and poor investor protection**, where the gains from standardized reporting are largest [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **Adoption timing and implementation quality matter**, as the Latin American study shows that well-timed and well-implemented adoption can yield clearer economic consequences [N2-F2].
- **The literature cautions against overinterpreting results**, because omitted variables, reverse causality, measurement error, sample selection, and nonrandom adoption can affect the observed effects [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3][N3-R3].

In short, mandatory IFRS adoption is more likely to improve liquidity and reduce the cost of capital when it is implemented in settings with weaker governance and higher information asymmetry, and when the effects are measured in ways that control for concurrent changes and institutional context. The evidence is strongest for liquidity and equity capital, but it remains heterogeneous and should be interpreted cautiously across studies and countries [N1-F1][N5-F3][N2-F2].
